turns.t: Come in, Cormac, sit yourself down. Hello, Mrs Fitzgerald. I've the letter here from the school nurse about the sports medical, and I've the notes from your last visit beside it, so we've a few bits to get through.
Hi.
Morning, doctor. He's been very good about coming, but he's not one for talking, as you know.
Sure that's no harm at all. Cormac, in your own words, what's the letter about?
Um. A check-up. For the hurling squad.
Right, so a general check-up before the new season starts. And is there anything you'd like me to be looking at while you're here?
No. Not really.
I'd say he'd tell you nothing if his arm fell off, doctor.
Ah well, then I'll do the asking and you do the answering. Are you on anything regular, any tablets or inhalers?
The blue inhaler.
And what's that one for, Cormac?
The asthma.
Good man. And how often would you be using it these days?
When I need it. Not much.
Okay. Any trouble with your breathing at all when you're running about the pitch?
No. It's fine.
Grand. Now, I can see in the notes that you had your tonsils out. When was that, do you remember?
When I was seven.
He was seven, yeah. He lived on ice cream for a week afterwards and was delighted with himself.
The best part of any operation, so it is. Now, do you have any allergies, Cormac, to medicines or anything else?
No.
None at all, good. And who's at home with you these days?
Mam and my little brother.
That's a busy house, I'd say. And what do you get up to outside of school?
Hurling. Three nights a week.
And on the other nights I'm the taxi service, so I am. Up and down to the pitch and back.
Well, that's what it takes. Right, I'll get your measurements now. Hop up on the scales for me and stand tall against the wall.
You're 172 centimetres tall, and you're 61 kilograms.
Is that good?
It's just a number for the file, nothing to be worrying about. Now, I'll put the cuff on your arm. Sit back and keep the arm nice and still for me.
Blood pressure is 112 over 68. Your heart rate is 64 beats per minute, and the oxygen in your blood is 99 percent.
Okay.

Now, because this is a sports medical and you're growing quickly, I'd like to do a few tests. First, I'd like to get a blood test for your iron levels, since lads your age training hard can run a bit low.
Do I need a needle?
You do, just the one, and it's over in a minute. The nurse is very good with it.
He's grand with needles, doctor, it's the fainting at the sight of blood that's the trouble, and that's me, not him.
Then you can wait outside for that part, Mrs Fitzgerald. Next, let's get a urine sample from you before you leave today. It's a simple check that the kidneys are fine for sport.
Okay.
And last one. I'd like to book you in for a spirometry test, that's the breathing test where you blow into a tube as hard as you can, so we know how your lungs are with the asthma.
Like blowing out candles?
Exactly like that, only harder, and three times in a row. You'll be well able for it.
When will we hear about the blood results?
The surgery will phone you in about a week. For the meantime, keep the blue inhaler in your kit bag at every training session and drink plenty of water, Cormac.
I will.
And I'd like to see you again in six months, just to check you're growing along nicely and the season's treating you well.
Six months, that's no bother. Will I book at the desk?
You will, on your way out. They'll give you the forms for the blood and the urine as well.
Can I go now?
You can, Cormac. Thanks for putting up with all the questions, and good luck with the hurling.
Thanks very much, doctor. Come on, you, and say thank you.
Thanks.

social_history.description: Lives with mother and younger brother

review_of_systems.details: No trouble with breathing when running

procedures_and_investigations.name: blood test for your iron levels

Keep the inhaler in the kit bag at training and drink plenty of water
